topic_summaries.Global Climate Politics and COP Negotiat:
• The Guardian dominates COP31 coverage, framing the pre-Cop summit in Fiji through multiple angles: Australia's leadership ambitions, low turnout from non-Pacific nations, and Turkey's methane hypocrisy as host
• The Independent emphasises justice and accountability, highlighting Pacific islands' legal demands and Trump's obstructive role; The Guardian similarly flags Bolsonaro's electoral advance as a threat to climate diplomacy
• The i and GB News sidestep COP negotiations entirely, focusing instead on trade and economic angles — EV tariffs and Brexit-EU friction — rather than the diplomatic climate agenda
topic_summaries.Yorkshire Drought and UK Weather Disrupt:
• BBC emphasises no immediate customer impact, noting Yorkshire Water won't introduce restrictions despite the drought declaration
• GB News adds hyperbolic framing, claiming "unprecedented" temperatures and linking the drought to record-breaking heat — claims not present in the BBC source
• Sky News source text inaccessible, yielding no usable content for comparison
topic_summaries.El Niño and Extreme Weather Outlook:
• BBC and The i take a fact-checking, cautious tone on UK snow claims; Metro and Evening Standard lean into alarming "Godzilla" and "polar vortex" framing, with Evening Standard even advising Londoners to stockpile food
• The Guardian focuses predominantly on international impacts — California flooding, Australian heat, New Zealand glaciers — while The Independent covers both UK forecasts and global adaptation stories
• Daily Mail amplifies dramatic scientific warnings ("super-duper," "Earth is almost entirely in the red") but its source text is heavily diluted by unrelated celebrity and news sidebar content
topic_summaries.Atlantic Hurricane Season 2026:
• BBC frames Isaias as an emerging, developing threat; The Guardian focuses on the moment of intensification into hurricane status
• The Independent covers the storm post-landfall, emphasising immediate impact ("slams," "powerful winds," "dangerous flooding"), while BBC and The Guardian report on forecasts and anticipated risk
• All three outlets cover the same storm, but differ in timing: BBC and The Guardian at the forecasting stage, The Independent after landfall
topic_summaries.UK Energy Crisis and Net Zero Debate:
• GB News dominates coverage with a sceptical, alarm-driven framing — linking net zero to national security threats, energy shortages, strike risks, and financial costs to consumers and taxpayers
• The Guardian challenges anti-net zero arguments directly, reporting a near-£500bn Conservative costing error; the Evening Standard echoes this counter-framing by noting business support for fossil fuel phase-out
• The i offers a positive, consumer-focused angle on green energy through a "zero-bills home" case study, contrasting sharply with GB News's crisis-led narrative
topic_summaries.Penguin Colony Collapse and Wildlife Dec:
• The Guardian and BBC both cover the chinstrap penguin colony collapse, but The Guardian emphasises ecological vulnerability while BBC foregrounds the statistical decline (63% fewer nests)

• The Guardian also broadens the frame to wider wildlife despair, referencing the 73% global wildlife drop from the Living Planet Report, adding emotional and contextual weight absent from BBC's reporting

• The Independent and The i diverge entirely from the penguin story — The Independent covering American river health, The i focusing on UK illegal waste dumping — reflecting little editorial consensus on the topic
topic_summaries.Australia Climate Litigation and Coal Mi:
• The Guardian leads with community activism and legal strategy, foregrounding the local Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook group and calls for further litigation; The Independent frames it more neutrally as a historic institutional ruling
• The Guardian's opinion piece frames the ruling as a warning to fossil fuel producers broadly, adding an advocacy tone absent from The Independent's straight news coverage
• All outlets agree on the core facts — MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant expansion rejected — but The Guardian spreads coverage across multiple angles (community, legal commentary, opinion) suggesting stronger editorial investment in the story

GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane, hammering communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surges.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore and by early Saturday was no longer considered a hurricane as its wind speeds continued to decrease.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region.”





Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and into southern Georgia.
“We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House late Friday night as he returned from a rally in upstate New York, adding that it was “under control.”

Flood warnings have been issued across multiple areas of England as a mix of autumnal weather is set to bring rain, storms and sunshine over the next week. 



Temperatures are forecast to rise over the coming week while wind from the northwest will bring showers particularly in northern and coastal areas on Saturday.



The week will see a “changeable but mild spell of weather” Greg Dewhurst, senior operational meteorologist at the Met Office told The i Paper, as Atlantic weather systems bring rain and strong winds.





Over the weekend, forecasts suggest high pressure and Atlantic air will result in cooler conditions, with the possibility of overnight frost. 



Sunday is likely to be bright and sunny with rain spreading into the southwest in the afternoon and strong winds hitting western coastal areas.



The Environment Agency has issued 10 flood alerts across areas of Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex. This is due to strong winds and high tides in coastal areas, which could see seafronts such as those near Clacton and King’s Lynn at risk of flooding over the weekend.

Gusts of 35-45mph along the coast are likely added Dewhurst, adding that no wind warnings have been issued by the Met Office. 



 
Unsettled and windy weather will continue into the week, with low pressure in the northwest bringing coastal gales on Monday night.  
Dewhurst added: “Despite the gloomy conditions, temperatures will remain mild and generally above average. 
“Low cloud is likely to be widespread, although rainfall will generally be light and patchy. A more organised band of rain is expected to arrive in Northern Ireland and western Scotland later in the day.” 
Temperatures are expected to rise on Tuesday, possibly reaching a high of 21 degrees Celsius in parts of England and Wales – above above the October average of around 14-17 degrees.  
“Tuesday sees a more active weather system move across the country,” said Dewhurst. While brighter conditions are expected in some areas of the country, Scotland and Northern Ireland in particular may see heavy and thundery rainfall with a risk of severe gales.  
While northern and western areas of the UK are expected to see heavy winds and rainfall for the remainder of the week, parts of England and Wales may see lengthy drier periods, including in regions already impacted by severe drought. 
Despite the rain expected for parts of the country, a drought was declared in Yorkshire on Friday after months of dry weather, resulting in low water levels in rivers and reservoirs and a drop in groundwater levels.



 
Water minister Emma Hardy said: “The recent rainfall is not yet enough to replenish all the water we’ve used over the spring and summer, and the Yorkshire drought declaration highlights the situation is still serious.” 
Parts of Scotland and Northumberland could see snow at the end of the week, with some forecasts pointing to snowfall of 4mm per hour on higher ground and peaks.

Deep inside an ancient woodland in Kent lies a vast clearing of barren land. Trees have stood at this site for centuries, but now lie dead across the floor. 



Until recently, this was the scene of one of the UK’s most notorious illegal waste dumps. Behind the trees, criminals created mountains of toxic waste that rose as high as 15 feet.



The site has now been cleared as part of a £15m clean-up operation by the Environment Agency (EA), which has removed 39,500 tonnes of household, commercial and medical waste in the past year. 





It’s part of a crackdown on a growing organised crime industry that is estimated to be costing England’s economy £1bn each year. Half of this is borne by the public purse, either through clean-up costs or lost revenue from taxes. 



‘We’re seeing more organised crime’ 



The term waste crime covers a range of offences, from small-scale fly-tipping to larger operations where criminals pose as legitimate businesses that collect waste for a fee, but then dump it illegally rather than paying to dispose of it properly.

“The nature and the scale of waste crime has changed quite a lot in the last five years or so,” said Matt Higginson, an environment officer at the EA who has overseen the clean-up at the site in Kent, known as Hoad’s Wood. 



 
“We are seeing more organised crime getting involved in it so that provides a greater challenge to the Environment Agency,” he said.  

Almost 40,000 tonnes of waste were cleared from Hoad’s Wood, but it will never be the same (Photo: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images) 
Matthew Scott, police and crime commissioner for Kent, told the House of Lord’s environment and climate change committee last year there was “absolutely no doubt” that organised crime networks, including individuals involved in modern slavery and drug dealing, were involved in large-scale waste crime. 
“These are people who are well versed in organised crime, and I believe that they act quite freely because they do not fear consequences,” he said.  
Authorities struggling to get a grip 
For several years authorities have struggled to get a grip on this growing underground industry. 
Illegal dumping in Hoad’s Wood was first reported to the EA in 2020, but the clean-up did not start until five years later. There was a significant increase in the levels of waste at the site around 2023, at which point the EA and Kent Police launched a joint investigation.   
Three men were arrested in February last year, but no one has been charged as of yet and the investigation is ongoing.

A record-breaking El Niño unfolding on the other side of the world is clearly raising the chance of extreme weather in London this winter, according to a top scientist.




Sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean have been recorded at 4C above normal, Japan Meteorological Agency revealed on Friday - the highest reading since records began.








The so-called “Godzilla” El Niño is worrying scientists and governments around the globe amid fears it will spark naturals disasters and extreme weather that will claim hundreds of thousands of lives.




Britain, along with much of Europe, should escape the worst of the impact as El Niños have a much stronger bearing on weather patterns in regions such as India, East Asia, South America and parts of Africa.




However the UK Government has warned that Britons face higher prices for foods like rice and coffee if harvests are badly impacted, while energy bills could also spike. 




The El Niño is expected to peak in December and last through to February 2027. 




In an interview with The Standard, Tim Stockdale, principal scientist at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), stressed that Britain’s “more variable” weather made it harder to predict how the El Niño will impact the UK over the winter. 


Members of London Fire Brigade assess the damage at a pub after Storm Katie hit the capital in March 2016
AFP/Getty




But he said the science was clear: there is a “greater likelihood” of more more extreme weather in the coming months. 













“There’s an expectation of the first part of the winter being milder, wetter and windier,” said Mr Stockdale. 




That could even be good news for southern England given this year’s drought, he added, with water levels needing to “recharge”, while also providing plenty of wind power. 









“Later winter is a more complex story, although big El Niño events can be associated with colder weather. It is variable (but) the probabilities are there.




“Where the balance of things will be in later winter, I don’t feel confident about it.” 




The last “super” El Niño to hit London during the winter of 2015/26 and subsequent spring brought damaging storms and freezing weather to the capital.

Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns


Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers




The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in world surfing reserves (WSR) found more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands.

The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.
The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.


View image in fullscreen
Croyde’s heavy wave is considered the best beach break in the UK. Photograph: Rob Tibbles
The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study.


Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.
Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The point breaks at Noosa in Australia are among those at most at risk. Photograph: Luke Sorensen

articles.title: Giant solar farm the size of 1,200 football pitches approved despite losing fertile arable farmland for 60 years
articles.raw_rss:
A solar farm the size of Heathrow Airport has been approved, despite the scheme meaning that swathes of arable farmland will be lost for 60 years. Green Hill Solar Farm will cover almost 3,000 acres of land across Northamptonshire and could power 200,000 homes when operational. But more than two-thirds of this land - the size of almost 1,200 football pitches - falls on "best and most versatile" (BMV) soil, the type most suitable for growing crops. This cannot be used for arable farming for the 60-year lifespan of the project. Ten acres of this BMV could be lost to farming permanently because of work needed to accommodate a battery storage site and a substation.

Britain’s fading hopes of a Brexit reset bargain with the EU covering university tuition fees and access to controversial ‘Made In Europe’ plans have been dealt another blow amid European “panic” over Chinese imports.



The UK had hoped to delay talks on lowering tuition fees for European students until next year. That way the two sides could negotiate on British calls to be included in Brussels’ protectionist Made In Europe plans at the same time, with the EU not yet ready to discuss the issue.



But the suggestion of delaying negotiations on fees so European students pay much less than full international rates was rejected strongly by several member states when it was floated by the European Commission recently, according to one EU source.





Cash-strapped British universities are against lowering fees.

The UK wants to be part of the Made in Europe scheme, which would favour European businesses, and had been hoping to negotiate inclusion for a concession on tuition fees.

articles.title: Drought declared in Yorkshire after dry weather
articles.raw_rss: Environment Agency says Yorkshire saw its fifth driest period on record between April and September.
articles.raw_meta: Environment Agency says Yorkshire saw its fifth driest period on record between April and September.
articles.jina_text:
The Environment Agency (EA) said low water levels in reservoirs and rivers had triggered the move despite recent rainfall across parts of the region.
Yorkshire officially entered drought status on Friday after a lack of spring and summer rainfall, having previously been classified as in a period of prolonged dry weather.
Yorkshire Water said it was not planning to introduce water restrictions for customers at this stage despite the drought declaration.
Andy Shaw, head of water production, treatment and energy at Yorkshire Water, said the EA's decision reflected dry conditions across the region but "does not mean water restrictions are currently needed".
EA manager Vicki Townend said Yorkshire had seen its fifth driest period on record between April and September.
Townend said: "The ongoing lack of rainfall means the flow in rivers and groundwater levels in certain parts of our area are very low and have now reached our trigger for declaring a drought.
"Even if we receive a few weeks of rain, we cannot quickly reverse the effects of the lack of rainfall during a very dry spring and summer."





Image caption, 

Baitings reservoir near Ripponden remains at a low level despite recent rain




She added: "We will continue to closely monitor the situation and implement our Yorkshire Drought Plan.
"As we see more impacts from climate change, heavier rainfall and drier summers will become more frequent. 
"We encourage people to be aware of the impacts of drought and use a little less water to speed up the recovery from drought."
Water Minister Emma Hardy said: "The recent rainfall is not yet enough to replenish all the water we've used over the spring and summer, and the Yorkshire drought declaration highlights the situation is still serious.
"Long-term resilience against our changing climate is a priority for this government."



Analysis by Paul Hudson, climate correspondent




Following the hottest and one of the driest summers on record, rainfall continued to be below average through September.
East Yorkshire was the driest area anywhere in the UK last month, with some locations recording less than 20% of expected rainfall.
Reservoirs are currently just above 40% capacity, well below the average for the time of year - and interestingly lower than they were at this time last year when a hosepipe ban was in force.
Groundwater levels are also very low across the chalk aquifers of East Yorkshire.
Drought status would in theory allow Yorkshire Water to reduce the flow out of some reservoirs which would normally replenish water courses, in order to slow their decline, and even apply for a hosepipe ban.
But because of the time of year, when demand for water in general falls as we head through autumn and winter, and rainfall normally increases, Yorkshire Water is not expected to apply for any restrictions.

View image in fullscreen
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images


Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence


‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji




Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.
But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.

Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.
Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.


View image in fullscreen
Fijian dancers perform at the summit’s welcome ceremony. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images
Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.
But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.
On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.
In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

articles.title: Will Super El Niño bring ‘a wall of snow’ to the UK? All the claims, fact checked
articles.raw_rss: From the polar vortex to Sudden Stratospheric Warming – all you need to know about the latest climate turmoil
articles.raw_content:
There have been a series of dramatic claims about the impact of Super El Niño – the climate phenomenon building in the Pacific Ocean.



El Niño is a regular shift in climate pattern, bringing changes to worldwide weather as warmer conditions spreads across central and eastern Pacific – but it has been predicted that this year, it is likely to be at its strongest since the 19th century.



Usually it does not have a great impact on the UK, instead causing major weather changes in South America, south-east Asia, southern Africa and Australia. Climate scientists now predict 451,000 people across the world will die due to additional heat.



But due to the size of this year’s event, there are fears that a Super El Niño could cause extreme changes to the weather in Britain – including speculation over a “551-mile wall of snow”.





Some have claimed there is risk that violent weather could bring chaos to transport and the economy – and even disrupt food supplies from other countries.



But how accurate are the claims? Here are some of those being made.



‘Polar vortex of snow and storms’



Much of the recent coverage of El Nino has centred around the impact that it will have on the polar vortex – strong westerly winds high in the stratosphere that encircle the North Pole every winter.



The vortex forms when the air high above the North Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter, then meets warmer air further south –  driving the fierce winds.

El Niño is a regular shift in climate pattern, bringing changes to worldwide weather as warmer conditions spreads across central and eastern Pacific – but it has been predicted that this year, it is likely to be at its strongest since the 19th century.



Usually it does not have a great impact on the UK, instead causing major weather changes in South America, south-east Asia, southern Africa and Australia. Climate scientists now predict 451,000 people across the world will die due to additional heat.



But due to the size of this year’s event, there are fears that a Super El Niño could cause extreme changes to the weather in Britain – including speculation over a “551-mile wall of snow”.





Some have claimed there is risk that violent weather could bring chaos to transport and the economy – and even disrupt food supplies from other countries.



But how accurate are the claims? Here are some of those being made.



‘Polar vortex of snow and storms’



Much of the recent coverage of El Nino has centred around the impact that it will have on the polar vortex – strong westerly winds high in the stratosphere that encircle the North Pole every winter.



The vortex forms when the air high above the North Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter, then meets warmer air further south –  driving the fierce winds.

Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat




The most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks of extraordinary harm.
The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid.

Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both.
But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law.
I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder.
The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels.
On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked justice Elena Kagan.
Chief justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts.
In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn.
And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf Coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis.
Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI.
If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook for tens if not hundreds of billions of dollars in payments to those who are harmed.

Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season


Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding




Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.


View image in fullscreen
People pick up sandbags in Mobile, Alabama, in preparation for Hurricane Isaias. Photograph: Octavio Jones/AP
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.
In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

The final decision rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, although the scheme has raised national security concerns over the Government’s drive to expand renewable energy under Net Zero.In a letter to planning officials, the MoD’s Defence Infrastructure Organisation warned that the development would cause “unacceptable interference” to radar systems at RAF Leeming and Brizlee Wood.

The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech.

Justifying the Conservatives’ decision to scrap the target of the UK reaching net zero emissions by 2050, introduced under Theresa May, the document says that estimates of how much this would cost the economy “have varied enormously”.






All hail the Death Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives
John Crace


Read more
It goes on: “In 2020, the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn.” It cites the Sixth Carbon Budget produced by the CCC, the government’s climate change advisers, saying the report put gross economic costs at £1.4tn, falling to £957bn when savings were taken into account.
However, the figures in the report in fact total £478bn, half of what the Tory document said. The error appears to have arisen because a tally of all the costs in a CCC spreadsheet from the document also included the row showing totals for each individual column, thus doubling it.
A CCC spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise this number. The committee has previously offered to meet with Ms Badenoch and talk her through our advice. That offer is, of course, still open.”


The committee’s most recent analysis puts the expected cost of achieving net zero by 2050 at about £110bn, or about £4bn a year – 0.2% of GDP.
The error was spotted by the publication Carbon Brief, which informed the Guardian.
It is possible the Conservatives copied the figure without checking it. It appears to have been published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator.
The Conservative document says it is intended to be a precise diagnosis of the UK’s problems. It is modelled in part on The Right Approach, produced by Margaret Thatcher’s Tory party in 1976, which set out some of the economic ideas later used in the 1979 election.

How California is bracing for a winter of floods, fires and extreme storms all at once


The strongest El Niño recorded is expected to bring a cascade of hazards to a state still facing wildfire and heat risks, while budget cuts have weakened disaster response agencies 
 Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here




Before this year, the US National Weather Service had never issued a September coastal flood advisory for the San Francisco Bay Area. In the past month, it has had to issue two.
As flood water swallowed intersections and eroded beaches up and down the California coast last week, scientists and emergency managers warned that this is just an early signal of a coming tumultuous winter as an already exceptional El Niño continues to strengthen. It’s been called everything from “super” to “Godzilla”, as forecasters hammer home the message that conditions brewing in the Pacific Ocean could soon climb off the charts, and fuel extreme weather around the world.

Tens of millions could face food insecurity, and global food prices could be pushed higher. Climate scientists have projected that by February, more than 450,000 people around the world could succumb to spikes in temperature linked to the strong El Niño. Yet more deaths will be caused by floods and droughts, wildfires and rain.


More on all this, after this week’s most important reads.
Essential reads
 
 
Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say 
 
Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey 
 
To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark 
In focus


View image in fullscreen
On the frontline … California residents sweep back wet mud following storms in 2023. Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images


California is among the places most likely to be hit hard by the climate pattern. Models show a more than 90% chance that this El Niño will be “very strong”, with roughly a 75% chance that it will be historic, according to the latest forecast the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). Severe storms, landslides and destructive high tides are on the menu – and they could happen all at once.
The impacts will be a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. But the effects are also layering on top of conditions fuelled by the human-caused climate crisis. Officials hope that preparations already under way may ready the most vulnerable communities for a more extreme future.

articles.title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
articles.raw_rss: Solar tiles were touted as an attractive alternative to solar panels - why have they not taken off?
articles.raw_meta: Solar tiles were touted as an attractive alternative to solar panels - why have they not taken off?
articles.jina_text:
She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.
For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.
This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.
For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes.
Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.
Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

The Washington Post via Getty Images
Tesla abruptly stopped marketing its solar tiles in August














For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.
Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.
In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.
Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".
Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.
The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."
Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.
She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.





"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.
But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

articles.title: Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
articles.raw_rss: The developing El Niño may impact the UK's weather prospects this autumn and winter but cold conditions are far from guaranteed.
articles.raw_meta: The developing El Niño may impact the UK's weather prospects this autumn and winter but cold conditions are far from guaranteed.
articles.jina_text:
Widespread snow driven by a polar vortex is rumoured to be heading for the UK this autumn and winter. But is that really the case?
Headlines have been suggesting it is down to the effects of El Niño but the truth is much more complicated.
For the rest of the autumn, El Niño actually increases the chance of wet, mild and potentially stormy weather for the UK.
Later in winter it could shift the odds towards cold and snow, something that can be influenced by changes in the polar vortex but none of this is certain.



What is a polar vortex?




The polar vortex is a ring of strong westerly winds encircling the North Pole every winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) above the Earth's surface.
It forms because the air high above the Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter. The contrast with warmer air further south drives the very strong stratospheric winds that make up the polar vortex.
This is all going on high up in the stratosphere, far above the troposphere - where our weather actually happens. 
A strong polar vortex tends to encourage a strong polar jet stream in the troposphere.
This drives areas of low pressure from west to east, bringing mild air from the Atlantic across the UK with spells of wind and rain. The coldest air is essentially locked away to the north of us.





Image caption, 

Disruptions to the polar vortex can cause the jet stream to change shape increasing the chance of cold winter weather affecting the UK




Sometimes, however, the polar vortex can wobble, weaken or even reverse direction.
Over a period of days and weeks this can work its way down through the atmosphere influencing our jet stream, causing it to weaken, become more bendy or reverse.
It can deliver colder northerly or easterly winds which can bring the UK its coldest winter weather 
However, it does not always translate into changes in weather patterns at the Earth's surface. 
Equally, periods of a meandering jet stream and cold winter weather often occur without significant changes in the polar vortex.



What does El Niño have to do with it?




El Niño - the naturally-occurring climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean - is continuing to grow and by some measures is already the strongest on record.
The heat released from the warm Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere impacts weather patterns around the globe.
In autumn it increases the chance of wet and stormy weather in the UK - something that is reflected in the forecasts for this season.
In late winter, the waves of energy released by El Niño can move upwards through the atmosphere making it more likely that the polar vortex becomes disrupted, increasing the chance of ice and snow. 
However, the links are unclear and the evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest winter in three decades - and coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and was unseasonably warm.

articles.raw_meta: A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key, says science writer Helen Pilcher
articles.jina_text:
The new Living Planet Report is out. Published every two years, it assesses the health of the natural world and, historically, it’s made for gloomy reading.
Take 2024’s report, which showed global wildlife populations had plummeted by 73% in 50 years and that ecosystems were being pushed toward collapse.

After reading it, I retired to a dark room and drank gin, but every time I popped my head out, there was more bad news: heatwaves, floods, wildfires and mass coral bleaching.
So, when this year’s edition dropped, I braced myself. But there was a plot twist. Biodiversity is still being pummelled, but not everywhere. According to the new report, conservationists have prevented the extinction of 32 birds and 16 mammals since 1993, and the numbers of wild tigers, elephants and sea otters are stable or growing. The energy sector has historically been extremely damaging to the planet, accounting for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the report notes we have passed a positive tipping point in the energy system, with the transition to renewables snowballing and coal use declining in many wealthy countries.


I can therefore see why the report is titled The Science of Hope.
But pegging it on hope is a bold move. People who write about the natural world, myself included, face a difficult choice. Focus on the bad news, and risk shouting into a void where people simply don’t want to listen. Focus on the good news and risk peddling “hopium” – stories that dull the pain briefly but do little to spur action.
The report, however, isn’t talking about your average kind of hope. It’s talking about a geeky kind of hope rooted in psychological research.


View image in fullscreen
Numbers of South African elephants are up, the report has found. Photograph: Merten Snijders/Getty Images


The American psychologist Charles “Rick” Snyder spent decades studying hope and came up with a surprisingly practical definition. Hope, he argued, starts with a goal but also requires pathways, or ideas about how to get there, and agency: the belief that you can make a difference. To this, the Living Planet Report adds another ingredient: resilience – the capacity to keep going when progress stalls. Or, as British anarchist punk band Chumbawamba famously put it: you get knocked down, but you get up again.
We can illustrate this point by looking at New Zealand’s kākāpō, the world’s fattest, greenest, least-able-to-fly parrot. When non-native predators drove the kākāpō to the brink of extinction, conservationists didn’t waste time wishing its numbers back up. In the mid 1990s, they moved the remaining birds to predator-free islands, and when recovery was slow, they changed tack.

July 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data shows


Devastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this year




This July was the worst on record for wildfires in England, provisional data shows, with England experiencing a clear upward trend in the total number of wildfires recorded.
This summer has been a stark reminder of the vulnerability of the UK to climate breakdown, after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.

Provisional government data reveals 1,354 wildfires have been recorded so far this year, with 624 of these in July alone, making 2026 the second worst year on record.
July’s wildfires included a devastating fire that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.



The summer of 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office, with 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F) recorded, smashing the previous record of 34 days.
Scientists have said the record heat of 2026 has only been possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil-fuel burning.
This year also marks the first time in the data series, which runs from 2010–26, that a death has been recorded due to a wildfire.
This incident involved the death of a 70-year-old man after a fire burned in fields behind Berrington Road and Castle Gardens in Chipping Campden, Gloucestershire.
Last week, the Guardian revealed that the government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.
Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP for Orkney and Shetland and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said this raised “serious questions” about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground.


This year is the second worst year on record in terms of total number of wildfires, with the worst being 2022, when 1,592 were recorded. 2022 was also a record year for heat, with the UK recording temperatures of 40C for the first and only time.
The 2026 data covers January to August only, whereas the 2022 data covers the full 12 months. Despite this, 2026 has already had a record number of woodland and forest fires, with 88 recorded.
After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.

Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity

Howard Bryant


Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity




It’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did the Indiana Fever this season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances. Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter.
The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of the WNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option.



Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against an other, symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell, hasn’t been able to concentrate fully on basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018.
Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant or willing pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn.
She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins.

articles.title: I live in a zero-bills house – I’ve saved £6,000 in four years
articles.raw_rss: Fraser Jackson's house is effectively a mini power station. When demand on the grid is high, energy generated in his home can be sold back to the grid
articles.raw_content:
Many of us dread opening our energy bills, particularly in the colder months. But imagine opening your mail to discover your electricity bill is zero. 



For some people, like Fraser Jackson, it’s a reality. That’s because 73-year-old Jack­son was one of the first cus­tom­ers in Britain to move into a “Zero Bills” new-build house, where he and his wife are guaranteed to receive free home energy for up to 10 years.



A Zero Bills home is purpose-built to be energy efficient, with good insulation, triple glazing, solar panels, a heat pump, and a home battery. These technologies work together to power the home, and energy can be stored in the battery. It is effectively a miniature power station. Later, when demand on the grid is high, that energy can be used in the home or sold back to the grid.





In 2022, Octopus Energy launched a world-first Zero Bills tariff to let hundreds of customers move into these homes with the promise of no energy bills. Now other brands are catching on to rewarding customers this way: Santander launched the first high-street mortgage for these Zero Bills homes. The TV environmentalist Chris Packham outlined the threats to security, economy and health in the 50-minute national emergency briefing film screened in Westminster Hall, London. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News


Britons kept in dark about scale of climate crisis, say viewers of ‘first-of-its-kind’ emergency briefing


Nine out of 10 people felt motivated to act after watching film outlining threats to food security, economy and public health




The British government must be honest about the scale of the threat posed by climate and nature breakdown, researchers have said, after nine out of 10 people surveyed after watching a briefing on the issue felt more motivated to act.
Last November, in the “first-of-its-kind national emergency briefing”, nine experts gave stark assessments in Westminster Hall in London of the scale of the changes needed in the UK to adapt to the rapidly changing climate and ecological landscape.

The team behind the event crowdfunded to produce the People’s Emergency Briefing, a film outlining the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, the economy and public health.
The film, which has so far been viewed by an estimated 185,000 people at more than 3,400 screenings, calls on the government to stage a primetime, televised emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis.


Of the 13,000 people surveyed, 87% said watching the film made them more motivated to act. Watching the film is associated with a “substantial shift” in environmental understanding and concern.
Furthermore, 89% of people said the government should respond to the crisis with emergency-level mobilisation, similar to the Covid-19 pandemic or the second world war.
Prof Mike Berners-Lee, the chair of the National Emergency Briefing, said the threat from Covid-19 was easy for the public to understand when they were trusted with the facts.
The team is calling for a similar united emergency response delivered by independent experts and fronted by the prime minister.
In addition, 93% of those surveyed said the public was not being fully informed about the climate crisis and nature loss.
The government has previously been accused of hiding the truth from the public after refusing to publish a report from UK intelligence officers warning of the catastrophic impacts on national security from the collapse of vital ecosystems around the world.
Prof Lorraine Whitmarsh, from the University of Bath who led the research, said while most people were aware of some of the risks associated with the climate crisis, the “second-order risks” around national security, food supplies and impacts on the NHS were not so obvious.

For the climate conscious, the outcome was largely what was hoped for: the court ruled that the Independent Planning Commission, the body that approved the extension of Mount Pleasant open-cut coalmine’s life by 22 years – doubling its output to 21m tonnes a year until 2048 – did not do enough to consider the mine’s scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions or how they might be mitigated.

Scope 3 emissions, which cover broad indirect emissions, include those that are produced downstream when the mine’s coal is burned by customers. In the case of the Mount Pleasant mine extension, these emissions accounted for 98% of its estimated climate footprint.
If this welcome news conjures ideas of a unified judicial manifesto against the climate harms of fossil fuel production, I’ll encourage you to consider it more moderately. It was a restrained and technical decision, split between three judges in favour and two against.


View image in fullscreen
Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group president Wendy Wales (centre), treasurer Tony Lonergan (right), Johnson Legal director Elaine Johnson (left) and Johnson Legal principal lawyer Anita O’Hart after their high court win in Sydney. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP
But even so, it sets a new baseline for coal and gas projects in New South Wales and potentially Australia-wide. Where the law requires decision-makers to consider a fossil fuel project’s greenhouse gas emissions, that should mean all of them, including scope 3.


The majority ruling rejected the idea that scope 3 emissions are someone else’s problem when they are emitted overseas. Scopes of emissions, as Justice Gordon noted, are just an accounting concept. “The impact of greenhouse gas emissions is the same, regardless of how they categorised.”
A majority of the judges also ruled that how emissions are counted under international treaties like the Paris agreement doesn’t answer the question whether the decision-maker should try to mitigate them. In essence, the entire carbon footprint of these projects needs to be assessed, including their downstream emissions.

World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’


Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis




The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica, increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.






Antarctica’s Zavodovski Island is home to the largest penguin super-colony in the world
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey.
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.


View image in fullscreen
A penguin colony below Mount Curry on Zavodovski. The island had the biggest colony in the world in 2011.  Photograph: Nicole Richters/British Antarctic Survey
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.


The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.

Chinstrap penguins are named for the black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek. Photograph: John Dickens/British Antarctic Survey

articles.title: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
articles.raw_rss: Climate change is blamed for dramatic decline of chinstrap penguins living on a remote volcanic island.
articles.raw_meta: Climate change is blamed for dramatic decline of chinstrap penguins living on a remote volcanic island.
articles.jina_text:
Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade. 
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.

Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.

British Antarctic Survey
The scientists used drones and trackers to study the penguin colony
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory. 





Advertisement












In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain. 
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds. 
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.


Watch: Secrets of Antarctica's giants
Climate change clues buried in Antarctic mud
Watch: Living alongside polar bears in a warming Arctic town
Where did all the penguins go? 

British Antarctic Survey
Macaroni penguin populations increased as chinstrap penguins declined










The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change. 
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards. 
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.



Hungry whales and active volcanoes
The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.













Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.

View image in fullscreen
Waves driven by swells from Hurricane Polo, crash over rocks in front of homes in the Capistrano Beach community. Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images


Landslides, flash floods and raging seas: is California ready for the ravages of El Niño?


A mix of natural disasters could all befall the state at once as it finds itself in the crosshairs of the climate phenomenon




On a cloudless autumn afternoon, sunlight sparkled on the water that had quietly swallowed a busy intersection to the north of San Francisco, as the surrounding rush-hour traffic slowed to a painful crawl.
There were no crashing waves or storm surges to blame for the flood. Marin county was one of many areas up and down the California coast affected by high tides last week, as parts of the Pacific swelled with excess warmth.

The submerged streets stood as an early signal of California’s vulnerabilities as it braces for what could be a tumultuous winter.
“If you think this is bad, just wait until December,” a state worker grumbled as he directed swarms of cars past the choke point toward a sidestreet.


Experts have warned that a potentially historic El Niño is brewing, with the power to unleash extreme weather around the world. The climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, is already under way, according to federal forecasters, and it is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.
California is poised to be in its crosshairs. Landslides, flash floods and encroaching sea levels are all on the menu – and they could all happen at once.


View image in fullscreen
A flooded highway intersection in Mill Valley, California, as high tides inundated parts of the coast.  Photograph: Gabrielle Canon/The Guardian


“What we’re really looking at is the compounding element,” Nick Brubaker, the chief resilience officer for the office of emergency management in Marin county said. The biggest concern isn’t just rising tides. It’s the way everything could collide.
Dangerous spikes in temperature are likely. Some areas could see supercharged storms and relentless rains. Others face explosive surf, strong currents and devastated marine ecosystems. The effects of El Niño will add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis there over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist.
And in recent wildfire burn scars, including the slopes of Big Sur that burned this summer and neighborhoods devastated by the 2025 firestorm in Los Angeles, there will be higher chances of debris flows.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026
articles.raw_rss: El Niño has led to an eerily quiet season so far but the first Atlantic hurricane of the year is now set to impact the southern USA.
articles.raw_meta: El Niño has led to an eerily quiet season so far but the first Atlantic hurricane of the year is now set to impact the southern USA.
articles.jina_text:
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year.
It is expected to reach hurricane strength late on Wednesday or early Thursday with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm.
It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Parts of Mexico could also see gusty winds and heavy rain as the storm moves northwards and eastwards.
Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led so far to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season with development suppressed by the historic El Niño that continues to grow in the Pacific.






Hurricanes: Inside the deadly storms




How strong will Isaias get?




In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias will strengthen rapidly and is likely to reach hurricane strength during Wednesday night. It will intensify further to a category 2 storm by Friday morning.
Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.
Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday.





Image caption, 

Damaging winds, torrential rain and coastal flooding are the major risks from the developing hurricane




Forecasters predict that 3-6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to the north-west of Florida.
A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.
Dangerous winds are anticipated with the chance of a storm surge which could inundate low-lying coastal areas.
The US National Weather Service says it expects to issue Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches later on Wednesday with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis declaring a state of emergency across 25 north Florida counties over concerns about potential impacts.
As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather.
Between 1-3in (25-75mm) of rain is forecast for large swathes of the south-east USA - as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas - with isolated totals of 5in (125mm).




Image source, Cristobal Herrera-Ulashkevich/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Image caption, 

Hurricane Milton was the last hurricane to make landfall in the USA, in October 2024. No hurricanes made landfall in 2025

Forecasters in the US predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average due to the developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean.

The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour?

Andy Beckett



On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins




Only a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching to the Greens in huge numbers, Green candidates were winning across the country, and the party was second behind Reform UK in some national polls.
Like Reform, the Green party presented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.

After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at the party’s bustling conference in Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success, such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.


This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, where Polanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmer in Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards, a Green win is not impossible.
But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners


Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not lead to success at polls




More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.

The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.



The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.


View image in fullscreen
Flavio Bolsonaro has shown he is as willing as his father, Jair, to curb nature protections and allow Indigenous territories to be exploited. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP


Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.
If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.

Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. articles.jina_text:
Jaguar has revealed its new electric car two years after its controversial rebranding sparked a backlash with the firm accused of going "woke".
The unveiling of the all-electric Type 01 is a gamble for parent company JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.
The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.
But it comes at a hefty price tag with a minimum cost of £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US.
The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.
The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".
However, the unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions on social media.
"Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design.





Advertisement












Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that the new design was an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looked like a hearse and lacked any "memorable Jaguar flourish".
But car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 looked "incredible" and made him "proud to be British".
"Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X.
Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising".
"If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC.
But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular, he added.
'Woke' furore
This launch was always bound to attract attention, after the company caused waves with the initial unveiling of its new direction.





In 2024 Jaguar released a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in the ad at all.
Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to show off a pair of radical concept cars, in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. 
Concept cars are mock-ups built to demonstrate an idea, rather than to work when on the road.
Acknowledging that they might prove controversial he quipped: "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody".

A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high court case has been described as a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that exported greenhouse gas emissions “cannot simply be ignored”.
On Wednesday morning, the nation’s highest court ruled that the approval of MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine expansion in NSW’s Hunter Valley was invalid, in a judgment that sets a precedent for fossil fuel projects in the state.

The coal company brought the high court case after a local community group, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg), halted the coalmine expansion on climate grounds in the NSW court of appeal.







Hunter Valley community group wins landmark high court climate change case over coalmine

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burnt overseas. Known as scope 3 emissions, these are not counted in Australia’s domestic tally.
Commenting on the judgment, the deputy Greens leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said: “For too long, big coal and gas companies have tried to pretend that the emissions from their products are someone else’s problem once they leave Australian shores. They’re not.
“When Australian coal is burned overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port. It comes back to communities here through worsening heat, drought, bushfires and floods.


“This judgment sends a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that the climate impacts of their projects cannot simply be ignored or pushed down the line.”
NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson, formerly a public interest environmental lawyer, also said the high court judgment could lead to “significant legal difficulty” for the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension, which was approved by the IPC a week ago.
